title: Five were waiting.
paragraphs:
Five were waiting.
All ten had lamps.
All ten looked the part.
All ten expected the Bridegroom.
But when the cry rang out at midnight, only five were ready.
Read that again.

This is not the story of atheists versus believers.
It is the story of people who were close to the wedding… but shut out of the door.

Jesus said it plainly in Matthew 25:10–12:
“And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut. Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.”
That verse should shake you.

Because the foolish virgins were not careless in appearance.
They had lamps.
They had expectation.
They had proximity.
They had a form of readiness.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Almost ready isn’t ready.

A lamp with no oil is religion without life.
A confession with no surrender is profession without possession.
A last-minute panic cannot replace a life that was never yielded to Christ.

The problem was not that they wanted in.
The problem was that they waited too long to prepare.
And that is where many people are living right now.

Church language.
Christian aesthetics.
Occasional conviction.
Delayed obedience.

You know the verses.
You know the songs.
You know how to look prepared.

But heaven is not opened by appearance.
The door does not swing on familiarity.
Jesus is not returning for people who admired truth from a distance while refusing repentance.

2 Timothy 3:5 warns of those who have “a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.”
That is terrifying.
Because you can stand near sacred things and still be spiritually empty.

Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this message is not here to entertain you.
It is here to wake you up.
And if this found you, it’s not by accident.

The foolish virgins discovered too late that borrowed oil does not exist in the kingdom.
You cannot live on your mother’s faith.
You cannot survive on your pastor’s fire.
You cannot enter by your spouse’s prayers.
You must know Christ for yourself.
And Scripture keeps pressing the warning.

Romans 3:23 says, “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Not some.
All.

That means the issue is deeper than being “unprepared.”
It is sin.
A heart alienated from God.
A soul that may speak His name and still resist His rule.

Then comes the weight of Romans 6:23:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

There it is.
Judgment and mercy in one line.
Death is earned.
Life is given.

So no, this parable is not a call to try harder in your own strength.
It is not moralism.
It is not “be better before Jesus comes.”
It is a warning that without the real life of Christ, you are not ready.

Because salvation is not produced by hustle.
It comes through grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says, “For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.”

The wise were ready because they had what the foolish neglected.
And spiritually, the only true readiness is found in Jesus Christ.

Not church attendance without transformation.
Not public image without private surrender.
Not delayed repentance.
Not emotional moments that never become obedience.

Jesus must become your righteousness.
Jesus must become your rescue.
Jesus must become your Lord.

Acts 3:19 says, “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.”
That is the doorway.
Repentance.
Not performance.
Not image management.
Repentance.
Then grace rushes in.
1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Do you see it?

The foolish virgins wanted access without preparation.
Many today want heaven without repentance.
They want comfort without the cross.
Hope without holiness.
A crown without Christ.

But Jesus is not mocked.
And the closed door in Matthew 25 is a preview of what happens when people keep postponing surrender.
Midnight always comes.

For some, it will be His return.
For others, it will be their final breath.

Either way, the question is not whether you once looked ready.
The question is whether you belong to Jesus now.
This is only the surface.

So examine yourself.
Not your branding.
Not your vocabulary.
Not your religious routine.
Your heart.

Are you truly in Christ?
Have you repented?
Have you trusted the finished work of Jesus?
Or are you still carrying a lamp with no oil?
2 Corinthians 13:5 says, “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.”

That is not condemnation for the broken who run to Christ.
That is mercy for the deceived who still have time to turn.

And here is the good news:
The same Jesus who warns is the Jesus who saves.
John 6:37 says, “Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”

Come now.
Not later.
Not when it feels convenient.
Not when the cry is already sounding.
Now.
Because almost ready isn’t ready.
